newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt seeks foreign scapegoats for church massacre.
newsitem.headline: Egypt seeks foreign scapegoats for church massacre.

text.p: Shaken by the massacre of 10 Christians in a southern church, the Egyptian authorities have looked abroad for someone to blame for the bloodshed.
Police say they are hunting down six local men, apparently militant Islamists, but at the same time official statements say no true Egyptian could commit such a crime.

The massacre last Wednesday, the bloodiest inside a church since the militant Gama'a al-Islamiya (Islamic Group) took up arms against the government in 1992, has reinforced a tendency to find foreign scapegoats for what most independent analysts believe is largely a domestic conflict.

Interior Minister Hassan el-Alfi this week revived allegations that Iran and Sudan continue to support the Gama'a al-Islamiya, the largest organisation fighting for a strict Islamic state. Iran and Sudan both deny this.

One of Alfi's ambitions for 1997 is to secure extradition from Europe and other parts of the world of Islamist leaders in exile. He constantly complains that European governments give such people political asylum and allow them to organise their followers inside Egypt from abroad.
The consultative chamber of parliament, in a long debate on political violence, has concentrated on what a working paper calls "The Foreign Dimensions of the Phenomenon of Terrorism".
Members have called for Draconian measures against foreign states that refuse to hand over Egyptian fugitives and for tighter controls on bank transfers from abroad.
Foreign Minister Amr Moussa, in a speech to parliament on Monday, said the time had come to hold the international conference on "terrorism" which Egypt has long advocated.
Speaking of the attack on the church in Abu Qurqas, he said: "The aim was not to ignite sectarian strife. The target was the security and stability of the Egyptian people."

The government newspaper al-Akhbar, in a front-page editorial on the subject on Tuesday, dismissed the gunmen who broke into the church as "agents of Egypt's enemies...unhappy with Egypt's progress and political stature".
"They do not belong to the soil of the country or to the honest people of Egypt...They are hired killers who have sold themselves to the devil of criminal extremism," it added.
"It is no accident this accident coincides with attacks on Egyptian positions by Egypt's enemies and dubious publications in league with Israel and the Jewish lobby," it said.
Foreign analysts say that the Egyptian authorities may be putting the cart before the horse by concentrating on the foreign links of the Gama'a, which undoubtedly do exist.
"The Gama'a has domestic roots and foreign branches, not foreign roots and domestic branches," one diplomat said.
"In the end the problem of political violence will be solved at home. Once that happens, any Gama'a leaders left in exile will run out of followers at home," he added.

The independent Egyptian Organisation for Human Rights (EOHR), in its analysis of the massacre, said the Gama'a might have changed tactics and adopted a deliberate policy of trying to set Copts against Moslems and vice versa.

The Gama'a has attacked Copts in the past but of about 1,100 people killed in the five years of political violence, some seven percent were Copts -- less than the proportion of Christians in the Egyptian population as a whole.
If sectarian strife was the aim of the militants, the Egyptian authorities have acted swiftly to stop that happening.

The Grand Sheikh of al-Azhar, the mufti -- the country's highest Moslem spiritual advisor -- and Religious Endowments Minister Mahmoud Hamdi Zakzouk all went to Abu Qurqas to offer their condolences to the bereaved Christian families.
Their message was that Egyptian society made no distinction between Moslem and Copt. The Christian church hierarchy, which almost always avoids confrontation, heartily concurred.

For a society where religion still counts and where religious extremism is a political force, the Egyptian establishment has managed to keep relations between Moslems and Copts remarkably peaceful over the years.
But the human rights organisation said the authorities must try harder. "EOHR urges (them) to promptly take positive steps that would promote tolerant values," it said.
